source: Gema et al. (2025, TMLR) Inverse Scaling in Test-Time Compute
finding: Longer reasoning by reasoning models lowers accuracy on some tasks (distractor counting, regression with spurious features, constraint-tracking deduction). Few-shot examples removed the spurious-feature failure for most models.
numbers: Claude Opus 4 on Misleading Math: accuracy falls from near 100% to about 85-90% as reasoning lengthens. DeepSeek R1, natural overthinking, 5 distractors: 70% to 30%. Grades Regression: all models have lower RMSE with few-shot examples; few-shot examples eliminate inverse scaling for all Claude models and for o3. o3-mini keeps inverse scaling even with few-shot; o4-mini is stable. 4 task families, 5 failure modes.
quote: extended reasoning causes models to shift from reasonable priors to plausible but incorrect features
limits: Tasks were built to break models, so rates are not typical. Task families are closed-form (counting, regression, puzzles), not open design or dilemma tasks. Reasoning length is set by prompt or budget, not by task type.
agent_relevance: Answers gap 5 only in part: reasoning models are not immune to harm from more thinking. Examples helped here because the task had a ground-truth signal to anchor on (closed-form regression). Do not read it as support for examples on open tasks. Supports a cap on thinking length and a distractor-resistance check.

source: Li et al. (2025) When Thinking Fails: The Pitfalls of Reasoning for Instruction-Following in LLMs
finding: Explicit CoT lowers instruction-following accuracy in 15 models, including reasoning-tuned ones. Letting a trained classifier decide per item whether to reason recovered most of the loss. Letting the model decide for itself had high recall but low precision.
numbers: 13 of 14 models drop on IFEval with CoT; all drop on ComplexBench. Llama3-8B-Instruct 75.2% to 59.0% (-16.2 points). Reasoning-enabled vs base pairs (Claude 3.7 Sonnet vs Think, DeepSeek-V3 vs R1) score lower with reasoning on. Few-shot mitigation used only 4 (IFEval) or 3 (ComplexBench) examples and gave modest gains. Self-reflection helped 11 of 14 models on IFEval but hurt weak models and fell on 10 of 14 on ComplexBench. Self-selective reasoning improved 10 of 14 (IFEval) and all models (ComplexBench). Classifier-selective: validation accuracy 0.75-0.92, best and most consistent, but one classifier per model.
quote: explicit CoT reasoning can significantly degrade instruction-following accuracy
limits: Constraint-following, not open design. Reasoning-enabled vs base comparisons are not controlled (extra training). Exact per-pair values in Table 2 could not be read cleanly from the extracted text. Classifier is trained on the same benchmark distribution.
agent_relevance: Strongest direct evidence for gap 6 and the cost of misrouting: a task-type gate is worth having, but the model's own judgement of 'needs reasoning' over-triggers. The S0 gate should be cheap and should default to NOT adding long reasoning on constraint-heavy or format-heavy items.

source: Jiang, Sun, Goetz (2026) When Reasoning Hurts Legal Drafting: The Verbalization Bottleneck in Patent Claim Generation
finding: On patent-claim drafting (a structured but generative legal task), a step list followed silently (implicit CoT) helped GPT-4o. Writing the same steps out first (explicit CoT) made claims worse than implicit and lost technical detail.
numbers: GPT-4o human expert rating: implicit CoT +5.2 points over the standard prompt (logical structure +5.9); explicit CoT averages 2.2 points below implicit. Automatic: PatClaimEval 23.5 to 23.7 (implicit) then 22.5 (explicit); LLM-judge 75.9 to 76.5 (implicit) then 70.4 (explicit). Llama-3.1-8B explicit CoT is more than 10 judge points below implicit. Removing the logical-grouping step costs over 1.5 points on logical structure; removing any step costs over 1 point on average. Human evaluation on 80 sampled items.
quote: implicit CoT ... consistently outperforms explicit CoT
limits: GPT-4o and small open models, not reasoning-tuned. Claude Opus 4.6 was the judge. Human sample is small (80). 'Implicit' is an instruction only, so the model may or may not think silently. Zero-shot prompts, no examples.
agent_relevance: Bears on gaps 4 and 9: a named-step list with NO worked example helped a strong model on a less-structured legal task, in contrast with the checklist null in novice humans (K03). The gain needed the steps NOT to be written out. Test in the agent: steps as hidden planning versus steps as written output.

source: Liu, Bahja, Lee (2026) When Reasoning Supervision Hurts: TTCW-Based Long-Form Literary Review Generation
finding: Fine-tuning small models on reviewer-style reasoning traces for a creativity-rubric task made generation less stable. Without traces, reports almost always completed.
numbers: Report completion with trace supervision 85.9-90.9% versus near 100% without. 3,551 of 4,007 failed generations (88.6%) contain semantic repetition loops; only 2.5% are token-level degeneration. On 200 paired Qwen3-8B stories, loop rate 14.5% at greedy vs 4.5% at T=1.0 (p=0.000325), but QWK fell 0.4965 to 0.4815. Conditional on finishing, the trace adds QWK +0.042 (95% CI +0.034 to +0.050). Dataset 263,911 stories, 14 TTCW dimensions; models Qwen3-4B, Qwen3-8B, Nemotron-8B.
limits: Small models, supervised fine-tuning, model-generated labels, no human raters. This is about training on traces, not prompting a frontier model. The output format is fixed.
agent_relevance: Weak evidence for gap 5. Shows that explicit reasoning on a creativity-rubric task can cost reliability even when it adds some accuracy. For the agent: put a hard stop on reasoning length and a repetition detector in open mode.

source: Cooper and Velasquez (2026) Narration-of-Thought: Inference-Time Scaffolding for Defeasible Ethical Reasoning
finding: A five-step named narrative scaffold with no worked example (protagonist, stakeholders, two-step consequences, uncertainty, then commit) fixed two trace failures of plain CoT on moral dilemmas. A matched-budget verbose-CoT control kept part of the gain. This is a skill-level scaffold on an ill-structured task.
numbers: DailyDilemmas, 100 scenarios, 4 generators. Plain CoT: uncertainty suppression in 50-72% of outputs, stakeholder collapse in 15-31%. NoT cuts stakeholder collapse by 13-30 points to under 1%, and uncertainty suppression by 29-72 points to 1-24%. Matched-budget control: Cliff's delta +0.79 to +0.90 (stakeholder count) and +0.65 to +0.93 (uncertainty) for 3 of 4 generators; grok-4-1-fast-reasoning is the exception. Ablation (claude-sonnet-4-6, N=3, 30 scenarios): dropping Stakeholders -0.41 delta on stakeholder count; dropping Uncertainty -0.92 on uncertainty; dropping Consequences -0.22 on causal depth; dropping Protagonist or Commitment no effect. Cells of 515-1,999 coded samples.
quote: stakeholder collapse (the trace names at most one party with a stake in the outcome)
limits: Outcomes are trace features coded by an LLM judge, not whether the decision is better. No human raters. The verbose-CoT control also cleared the binary thresholds, so part of the gain is just asking for perspective-taking. N=1 per cell in the matched-budget test.
agent_relevance: Best LLM evidence for gap 4: the open-task gain can come from named heuristic steps alone, and each step carries its own effect (ablation). This favours skill-level scaffolds over example content on dilemma tasks. Still untested: does it improve final answer quality? Use as the model for the open-mode scaffold and add a judged-quality check.

source: Wang et al. (2025) From Harm to Help: Turning Reasoning In-Context Demos into Assets for Reasoning LMs
finding: Reasoning models do worse with few-shot CoT than with direct answering, and adding more exemplars makes it worse, even with high-quality R1 traces. Two causes: copying steps from a similar example, and failing to extract a strategy. Turning demos into stated insights, then solving without the demo in context, helps.
numbers: AIME'25: GPT-4.1 34.0 to 48.0 (+14.0); o1-mini +2.7 (AIME), +1.7 (GPQA); R1-Distill-Qwen-7B +12.0 AIME, +4.8 GPQA (I2S+); Qwen3-1.7B +6.7, +3.5; R1-Distill-14B AIME 50.0 to 60.0, GPQA 59.5 to 63.03. Open-ended 'General' set (GPT-4.1 judge): R1-Distill-14B 57.68 direct to 66.64 (I2S) and 68.40 (I2S+); 7B 51.28 to 51.72 (I2S) but 49.28 (I2S+); Qwen3-1.7B 55.08 to 57.16. 'Engineering' set gains are small (7B 40.04 to 40.24; 14B 49.44 to 51.04). I2S uses three question-conditioned calls and is compared with majority@3.
quote: high textual similarity leads the model to treat the target as the same as the exemplar
limits: Mostly closed-form math and science. Open-ended sets are judged by GPT-4.1 against a GPT-4.1-written reference, which the authors say can penalize valid variants. Gains on the open sets are small and mixed. Demonstrations were R1 traces, not human worked cases.
agent_relevance: Main support for gaps 2 and 8: near-identical examples can mislead strong reasoning models (copying), and the fix is to abstract the example into an explicit principle first (skill, not topic), then solve without the example visible. Matches K05. Use this order in O1: extract the principle, drop the example text, then solve.

source: Ge et al. (2025) Innate Reasoning is Not Enough: In-Context Learning Enhances Reasoning LLMs with Less Overthinking
finding: Opposing result to d06 on math: zero-shot and few-shot CoT help R1-distilled models in most cases. The size of the gain depends on model size and problem difficulty. One-shot beat five-shot.
numbers: R1-Distill models 1.5B-32B, six math sets. CoT raises accuracy in 72% of model-by-dataset cells. R1-32B: +0.6% to +23.1% on easy sets (GSM8K, ASDiv, SAT_MATH), +33% to +333% on hard sets (MATH, AIME24, AMC23). R1-1.5B shows the reverse: +53.3% to +475% on easy sets, none to +300% on hard. Reflection counts cut by about 90% in some cases. One-shot CoT consistently better than few-shot (default few-shot was five-shot).
limits: Math only. Percent gains are relative and large because direct baselines for tiny models are very low. Distilled models, not frontier reasoning models.
agent_relevance: Gives a clean ability-by-difficulty interaction (gaps 2 and 10): the benefit of a scaffold depends on the model's baseline on that task. Large models gain little on easy items; small ones gain most there. For the agent: route by the model's own baseline, and prefer one example to many.

source: Tang, Tuncel, Koerner, Runkler (2025/2026) The Few-shot Dilemma: Over-prompting LLMs
finding: A dose-response curve for examples on a structured classification task: accuracy peaks at a modest number of selected examples, then falls. The turning point depends on the model and on how relevant the examples are.
numbers: Software requirement classification (PROMISE, PURE), 7 LLMs. Peak at roughly 5-20 TF-IDF-selected examples for GPT-4o, GPT-3.5-turbo, LLaMA-3.1-8B and Gemma-3-4B, then decline; DeepSeek-V3 plateaus; LLaMA-3.2-3B weakens earlier. LLaMA-3.1-8B reaches 95% weighted F1 with 10-20 examples, about 1 point above the earlier best. On a relabeled dataset peaks move to fewer examples. Declines are sharper in multi-class labeling.
limits: Closed-form classification, not open-form tasks. Similarity is by TF-IDF, so it measures near examples only. Distant examples are not tested.
agent_relevance: Partial answer to gap 8: even on a well-structured task the useful number of examples is small (5-20) and model-specific. For open tasks, expect the peak to be lower. Cap examples at 1-3 in the agent until a dose test on open tasks exists.

source: Zhang et al. (2025, COLM) NoveltyBench: Evaluating Language Models for Humanlike Diversity
finding: Frontier models give far fewer distinct answers than people. In-context regeneration (show the model its earlier answers and ask for a different one) restored human-level diversity; asking for creativity in a system prompt or paraphrasing barely helped. More reasoning effort in OpenAI models lowered diversity and utility.
numbers: 1,100 prompts (100 curated, 1,000 WildChat), 20 non-reasoning models. Larger models in a family are often less diverse than smaller ones. Claude 3 Opus, GPT-4o and Gemini 2.0 Pro over 8 generations roughly match 8 human writers with regeneration; GPT-4o and Gemini 2.0 Pro exceed human cumulative utility. System prompt and paraphrase only marginal. OLMo 2 post-training: each stage lowers diversity, biggest drop at DPO. o3 and o3-mini: more reasoning effort gives less diversity and less utility; Gemini 2.5 Flash budget has minimal effect.
limits: Human baseline is 8 authors from one institution. Regeneration is sequential, so it costs more tokens than parallel sampling. The reasoning-effort result is a trend shown in a figure, not tested for significance in the text.
agent_relevance: Closes part of gap 7: the example-free method that works is sequential 'show previous outputs, ask for new', which is fed by the model's own outputs, not by human examples. Also a second 2025 data point (with Sprague and Liu) that more thinking does not help open generation.

source: Jiang et al. (2025, NeurIPS D&B) Artificial Hivemind: The Open-Ended Homogeneity of Language Models
finding: Even with high-temperature sampling, one model repeats itself, and different models give near-identical answers. So sampling from several models is not a source of real diversity.
numbers: 26K open-ended queries from WildChat, 70+ models (25 shown), 31,250 human annotations with 25 raters per item. Same-model responses at top-p 0.9, T=1.0: average similarity above 0.8 in 79% of cases. Cross-model average similarity 71%-82%; DeepSeek-V3 vs qwen-max 0.82, DeepSeek-V3 vs gpt-4o 0.81. Across 42 models mean similarity 0.800 for high open-endedness prompts vs 0.837 for low. Paraphrased prompts 0.781 vs 0.821 within-prompt.
limits: Embedding similarity is a proxy for diversity. The paper gives no result on any scaffold that fixes it. Reward models and judges were found poorly calibrated to idiosyncratic human preferences.
agent_relevance: Gap 7: an agent that takes N samples or N sub-models for open tasks gets less independent variety than it appears to. Diversity must come from structure in the request (assigned directions, previous-output exclusion), and any LLM judge used to pick among candidates is itself miscalibrated on open tasks.

source: Wang et al. (2025) Route to Reason: Adaptive Routing for LLM and Reasoning Strategy Selection
finding: A thinking model beats its non-thinking counterpart on hard math but gives marginal gain or a slight drop on simple and commonsense tasks. A router that jointly picks model and strategy per query cuts cost with little loss.
numbers: QwQ vs Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct: large gains on MATH and OlympiadBench; marginal or slightly negative on GSM8K and MMLU. CoD prompting cuts answer length with comparable accuracy to CoT on easier tasks. Seven tasks (language understanding, scientific, mathematical reasoning). Exact router scores not extracted here.
limits: Routes by predicted difficulty and cost on benchmarks with answers; no open-form, creative or ill-structured tasks. Needs a trained router per model pool.
agent_relevance: Gap 6: published routers decide on difficulty, not on well- vs ill-structured. Nobody has measured the cost of sending an ill-structured task down the wrong path. An S0 gate for the agent would be a new design.

source: Zhou and Shbita (2026) Evaluating Ill-Defined Tasks in Large Language Models
finding: Position paper with two probes. Benchmarks for ill-defined tasks (complex instruction following, diagram drafting) give weak signal. Few-shot examples had inconsistent effects on a diagram-drafting task.
numbers: A trivial fixed-token baseline scores 17.55 on IFEval, close to GPT-2 at 19.72. ComplexBench judge-seed variance up to 2% and 2-4% shift by language. NL2Mermaid: Llama 3.1-8B logic 67.71 to 80.58, Granite 3.3-8B 58.90 to 73.90 after prompt changes, but the combined score fell. Few-shot raised some criteria but not the overall metric. No inter-judge agreement reported.
limits: Read through a fetch summary of the HTML page, not full text, so details may be missing. Small models. Not a controlled test of examples.
agent_relevance: Supports gap 6 and the need to measure open tasks with care: a metric that rewards format can look like progress. Use human or multi-judge checks before trusting any open-mode gain.

source: Instructional Science (2023) Better self-explaining backwards or forwards? Prompting self-explanation in video-based modelling examples for learning a diagnostic strategy
finding: A semi-structured diagnostic skill (car malfunction diagnosis). Modelling examples did NOT beat open problems on learning overall, but prompt type interacted with prior knowledge.
numbers: 78 automotive apprentices, 3 groups (examples with retrospective prompts, examples with anticipatory prompts, control with open problems). No overall advantage of examples over control. Higher prior knowledge learned more with anticipatory prompts; lower prior knowledge gained more self-efficacy and germane load with retrospective prompts.
limits: Read as an abstract only (Semantic Scholar record); author list not retrieved. Not a replication of Nievelstein in law; the domain is vocational diagnosis. No detailed statistics seen.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: the closest conceptual near-replication found, and it did not reproduce a simple example advantage. Suggests the worked-example benefit on less-structured tasks depends on prompt type and learner level, which fits K05.

source: Journal of Computer Assisted Learning (2024) Video-based modeling examples and comparative self-explanation prompts for teaching a complex problem-solving strategy
finding: Same diagnostic domain, larger sample. Modelling examples improved diagnostic knowledge and skills when scaffolds were present, but not independent skill without scaffolds. Comparative prompts looked promising only for higher prior knowledge.
numbers: 118 automotive apprentices, 3 groups (comparative prompts, sequential prompts, no examples). No effect on cognitive load. Knowledge and scaffolded skill improved; independent skill did not.
limits: Abstract only (Semantic Scholar record). Retrospective cognitive load measure. Not law, not Nievelstein's design.
agent_relevance: Gaps 3 and 10: a partial confirmation of the example benefit with a boundary (transfer to unaided performance is weak) and an expertise-reversal hint for comparison prompts. For the agent: test the unaided step after a scaffold, not only the scaffolded run.

source: BMC Medical Education (2017) Fostering clinical reasoning in physiotherapy: concept map study vs completion after example study in novice and advanced learners
finding: In a clinical-reasoning domain, concept-map completion after studying worked examples beat concept-map study for both novice and advanced learners on near and far transfer.
numbers: 61 second-year physiotherapy students, 130-min guided phase plus 4-week self-study. Completion vs study: near transfer p=.010, far transfer p<.001. Prior ability x condition interaction on conceptual knowledge but not on transfer.
limits: Abstract only. No example-versus-no-example comparison, so it does not test the worked-example effect itself; it shows an add-on to examples works for both levels.
agent_relevance: Gaps 3 and 10: no expertise reversal on transfer in a clinical domain, in line with K02, but this is about the add-on activity. Suggests pairing an example with a completion step may serve both weak and strong solvers.

source: Semantic Scholar citation scan of Nievelstein et al. (2013), Contemp. Educ. Psychol. 38
finding: Scan of the 93 citing records the service returned, searching titles and abstracts for ill-structured, less-structured, law and legal. No direct replication or failed replication of the law-student study appears.
numbers: 93 citing records. Only 4 hits on the keywords, none a replication (a legal-reasoning curriculum paper, an argument-mining tutor, a legal network paper, an algebra expertise-reversal paper). Closest domain extensions: d13, d14, d15, and a 2021 history-annotation study (102 undergraduates; labeled model annotations raised historical reasoning vs control).
limits: The service lists only some citing works and may omit non-indexed ones. Title and abstract keyword scan, not a full-text check. Absence of evidence, not evidence of absence.
agent_relevance: Gap 3 stays open. The anchor result is a single study; keep K01 and K02 at single-source.

source: Synthesis of d02, d05, d11: task-type gating for reasoning
finding: Across three 2025-2026 papers, three kinds of gate exist: model self-judgement (high recall, low precision), a trained per-model classifier (validation accuracy 0.75-0.92), and a difficulty router. None gates on well- vs ill-structured. Measured misrouting costs: -16.2 points (Llama3-8B IFEval) when CoT is wrongly applied; marginal gain or slight drop on easy tasks when a thinking model is wrongly used.
numbers: d02: classifier-selective is best on IFEval and ComplexBench except a minor drop for DeepSeek-V3 on IFEval. d11: the thinking model gives marginal gain or drop on GSM8K and MMLU. d05: on dilemmas the cost of plain CoT is trace failures (stakeholder collapse 15-31%, uncertainty suppression 50-72%).
limits: Cross-paper synthesis by this agent; each number comes from the paper cited in its own line. No study reports routing accuracy between structured and ill-structured tasks.
agent_relevance: Gap 6 stays partly open. Practical rule for S0: use cheap surface cues (is there a checkable answer, are there hard format constraints, is there a population of valid answers), bias to the safer default per class, and log misroutes so they can be measured.
